steps.title: Install pandas and load orders.csv
steps.instructions: Run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas`, download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial into the folder, then in main.py read it with pd.read_csv and print(df). Run `uv run main.py` to see the [40 rows x 9 columns] summary.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the pd alias
Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
The printed summary shows the shape

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip / pip3
Using a uv virtual environment (uv init, uv add, uv run)
Why import pandas as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV files and two-dimensional data
Loading a CSV into a DataFrame with read_csv

hints: Make sure pandas is installed in the environment you run from: `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas` / `pip3 install pandas`).
Put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py. You can download it from the GitHub repo linked in the description.
main.py needs three lines: `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')` and `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py`. The output should end with `[40 rows x 9 columns]`.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv environment, which gives ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
orders.csv is not in the working directory, which gives FileNotFoundError.
Typing `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read_CSV` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Using `pip install` on Mac/Linux when only `pip3` is available.
Forgetting `print(df)`, so nothing is shown when the script runs.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load the CSV in a notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb (Ctrl+Shift+P > New Jupyter Notebook); in cell 1 import pandas as pd and read orders.csv into df, in cell 2 print(df). Run both cells.

targets.caption: The new Jupyter notebook
Cell 1: import pandas and load orders.csv
Cell 2: print the DataFrame

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook via Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P > New Jupyter Notebook (or a .ipynb file)
Installing the VS Code Python extension to get notebook support
Cells run independently; df stays loaded between cells
Run above/below, deleting cells and clearing cell outputs

hints: Create a new Jupyter notebook (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P > "New Jupyter Notebook") and save it next to orders.csv as notebook.ipynb.
In the first cell write: import pandas as pd and df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv"), then run it and pick a Python kernel when asked.
Add a new cell below with print(df) and run just that cell; the table should appear underneath.
If running fails, install the Python extension from the Extensions pane and make sure pandas is installed in the kernel you selected.
common_mistakes: Creating a .py file instead of a .ipynb notebook, so there are no cells to run.
Missing the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so the "New Jupyter Notebook" command doesn't appear.
Selecting a kernel/interpreter where pandas isn't installed (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas').
Saving the notebook in a different folder from orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError.
Running the print(df) cell before the read_csv cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Typing pd.readcsv instead of pd.read_csv.
steps.run_command: Run cell 1, then run cell 2 (play button next to each cell in the notebook)
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In new notebook cells run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info() and df.describe(). Then inspect df.columns and df.index.

targets.caption: Preview the first five rows
Column names, non-null counts and dtypes
Summary statistics for numeric columns
RangeIndex from 0 to number of rows

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows
tail() shows the last five rows
info(): entries, columns and dtypes; why text columns show as object
describe() generates descriptive statistics (count, mean, quartiles)
df.columns lists column labels
df.index is a RangeIndex (start 0, stop 40, step 1)

hints: Make sure the cell that loads the CSV into df has been run first, then add a new cell below it.
Each of head, tail, info and describe is a method: call it with parentheses, e.g. df.head().
columns and index are attributes, not methods: write df.columns and df.index with no parentheses.
If only the last result appears, put each expression in its own cell, since a notebook cell only displays its final expression.
common_mistakes: Running the exploration cells before the cell that defines df, which raises NameError: name 'df' is not defined.
Writing df.head without parentheses, which prints a bound method instead of the table.
Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises TypeError: 'Index' object is not callable.
Putting several expressions in one cell and expecting all of them to display. Only the last one shows (info() still prints because it prints directly).
Expecting describe() to summarize text columns by default. It only shows numeric columns unless include='all' is passed.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: Select one column as a Series with df['Country'] and several with a list of names. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]['Country'].

targets.caption: Select one column to get a Series
A list of columns gives a DataFrame
Select a row by its position

explanations.topic: Selecting one column returns a pandas Series
Plain Python functions like len() and set() work on a Series
A list of columns returns a new DataFrame, not a Series
iloc selects rows by integer position
Row values can be read by position or by column name

hints: Use square brackets with the column name as a string: df['Country'].
For several columns, put a list inside the brackets, so you get double brackets: df[['Country', 'Product']].
Rows are selected by position with df.iloc[n]. Note that iloc uses square brackets, not parentheses.
Chain a column name after the row to get a single value: df.iloc[10]['Country'].
common_mistakes: Writing df['Country', 'Product'] with single brackets, which raises a KeyError.
Calling df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of df.iloc[0].
Misspelling or miscasing a column name (e.g. 'country'). Check the exact names with df.columns first.
Expecting df.iloc[1] to be the first row. Positions start at 0.
Using an iloc position at or above the row count (40), which raises an IndexError.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: Filter rows with a condition like df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics'], combine conditions with & and |, and compare numbers like df[df['Quantity'] > 2].

targets.caption: Filter rows where Category is Electronics
Combine conditions with & or |, each in parentheses
Numeric comparison filter

explanations.topic: Boolean mask: df[df[col] == value] keeps rows where the condition is True
Empty result because the wrong column (Product instead of Category) was filtered
Combine conditions with a single & inside parentheses, not Python's 'and'
Use a single pipe | for OR between conditions
Numeric comparisons: >, <, <=, != in filters

hints: Start with the condition alone: df['Category'] == 'Electronics' gives True/False per row; wrap it in df[...] to keep the True rows.
If you get an empty table, check that you're filtering the right column; 'Electronics' lives in Category, not Product.
To combine filters, wrap each condition in parentheses and join them with & (and) or | (or): df[(cond1) & (cond2)].
For numbers, compare directly: df[df['Quantity'] > 2].
common_mistakes: Using Python's 'and'/'or' instead of & and |, which raises 'The truth value of a Series is ambiguous'.
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when using & or |, causing operator-precedence errors.
Filtering the wrong column (e.g. Product == 'Electronics') and getting an empty DataFrame.
Mismatched capitalization of column names or values ('category', 'electronics', 'usa') leading to KeyError or empty results.
Comparing Quantity to a string like '2' instead of the number 2.

steps.title: Use string and isin filters
steps.instructions: Filter with .str.startswith('A') and .str.endswith('a') on the customer name column. Use .isin([...]) on Country and negate it with ~.

targets.caption: String method filter on Customer Name
isin filter on Country
Tilde reverses the isin condition

explanations.topic: String matching is case-sensitive (ends with 'A' returns nothing)
Using .str to access string methods like startswith/endswith
isin replaces a long combined OR condition
The ~ operator negates a boolean condition

hints: Text methods live under the .str accessor of a column, e.g. df['Customer Name'].str.something(...).
Wrap the condition in df[...] so it selects rows: df[df['Customer Name'].str.startswith('A')].
For several allowed values use df['Country'].isin([...]) with a list, inside df[...].
To get everything NOT in the list, put ~ in front of the condition: df[~df['Country'].isin([...])].
common_mistakes: Calling .startswith directly on the column without .str (AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'startswith').
Using uppercase 'A' with endswith and getting an empty result because matching is case-sensitive.
Passing values to isin as separate arguments instead of a single list.
Using 'not' or '!' instead of ~ to negate the Series condition.
Misspelling the column name (e.g. 'Customer name') and getting a KeyError.
steps.code:
df[df['Customer Name'].str.startswith('A')]
df[df['Customer Name'].str.endswith('a')]
df[df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]
df[~df['Country'].isin(['USA', 'Sweden', 'Brazil'])]

steps.title: Update data with loc
steps.instructions: Change values with df.loc[condition, 'Column'] = value (e.g. USA to United States), then uppercase a column with df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().

targets.caption: Locate rows by condition, then name the column to assign
Replace the column with its uppercased version

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label or condition, iloc by index position
loc with a condition returns a DataFrame because several rows can match
Adding a column after the comma assigns a value to that cell
A single loc assignment updates every row that matches
Assigning the result of .str.upper() back to the column updates the whole column

hints: The pattern is df.loc[<row condition>, '<column>'] = new_value.
The row condition is a boolean filter: df['Country'] == 'USA'.
Check the change by re-running the filter. Filtering on 'USA' should now return no rows.
For the whole column, use df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper(), then print df['Country'].
common_mistakes: Misspelling a column name (for example 'Product Name' instead of 'Product') creates a new column instead of updating the existing one.
Chaining brackets like df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ... triggers SettingWithCopyWarning and leaves df unchanged. Use .loc instead.
Calling .upper() without .str on a Series raises AttributeError.
Not assigning the result back: df['Country'].str.upper() on its own does not change df.
Re-running the 'USA' replacement after uppercasing matches nothing, because the values are now 'UNITED STATES'.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['Customer Name'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['Customer Name'] == 'Anna ...']

df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'USA']
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']

df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with df = df.drop(39), check with df.tail(), then reload the CSV. Use df.dropna(), df.fillna(...) and df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True), then display df.

targets.caption: Drop the row at index 39 and reassign df
Confirm row 39 is gone
Drop rows containing NA values
Fill missing values in place
Rename a column

explanations.topic: df.drop removes a row by its index label
dropna removes rows with null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing them
inplace=True modifies the existing DataFrame instead of returning a new one
Renaming columns with rename(columns=...)

hints: drop() returns a new DataFrame, so assign the result back to df before looking at df.tail().
After experimenting, reload the CSV with pd.read_csv so later cells start from clean data.
fillna and rename only change df itself when you pass inplace=True.
rename takes a dict: df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True).
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without reassigning, so the row still appears.
Re-running the drop cell after the row is gone, which raises KeyError: '[39] not found in axis'.
Expecting dropna()/fillna() without inplace=True to modify df.
Misspelling the column name in rename (e.g. 'OrderId'), which silently changes nothing.
Forgetting that later cells must use the new column name 'Order ID' after renaming.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# reload the data frame
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

df.dropna()

df.fillna({'OrderID': 0}, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save
steps.instructions: Run df['Country'].value_counts(), df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum() and df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False), then save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).

targets.caption: Count how often each country appears
Sum prices per country
Sort rows by price, highest first
Save the DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts gives a count of each distinct value
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY with an aggregate
Sorting descending with ascending=False
to_csv and the index parameter

hints: Each operation goes in its own notebook cell. Pick a column and call a method on it.
Count values with df['Country'].value_counts(). For totals per group, use df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum().
Sort with df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False). Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).
If you get a KeyError, check that the exact column names match df.columns. Capitalization and spaces matter, especially after the earlier rename.
common_mistakes: Leaving off the parentheses, as in df['Country'].value_counts. This shows a method object instead of the counts.
Forgetting to aggregate after groupby. You need .sum(), otherwise you only get a GroupBy object.
Expecting sort_values to change df in place. It returns a new DataFrame unless you reassign it or pass inplace=True.
Omitting index=False in to_csv. This writes an extra unnamed index column to the file.
Using a column name that was renamed earlier, such as 'OrderID' vs 'Order ID'. This causes a KeyError.
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
